reasoning_summary: The proof is a two-step citation chain and both steps survive counterexample search. Step 1 (lines 0001-0004) restricts the index set from I to J where all non-zero summands live; since every finite F subset I has sum_{i in F} v_i = sum_{j in F cap J} v_j and likewise for norms, no family can make one side absolutely net-convergent and the other not. Step 2 (lines 0006-0009) is the standard Banach-space fact that absolute net convergence over a countably infinite J is equivalent to absolute convergence of the series along an enumeration, with equal sums; absolute net convergence is the enumeration-independent condition sup over finite F of sum_{j in F} ||v_j|| < infinity, and absolute convergence in a Banach space forces unconditional convergence, so the limit is enumeration-independent. Refutation attempts using conditionally convergent series (alternating harmonic, where rearrangement changes the sum) fail because neither side converges ABSOLUTELY there; attempts using e_n/n in ell^2 (convergent but not absolutely) fail on both sides simultaneously. The stated corollary follows immediately by applying step 2 to two enumerations. The only defects located are in the problem statement rather than the reasoning: 'r in R_{>0}' is a type mismatch since the sum lies in V, and the enumeration is written {j_0, j_1, j_2, ...} while the series runs from n=1, a cosmetic indexing-convention off-by-one that the cited lemma inherits identically, so the two cited steps still compose correctly.
